CALIFORNIA INDIAN CHILD WELFARE ACT (CAL-ICWA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Riley Lee

CAL-ICWA INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND DECLARATION
I, Jordan Lee, am providing this information sheet in connection with a California proceeding involving Riley Lee, a minor born May 3, 2015, in which there is an indication that Riley Lee is or may be an “Indian child” as defined by the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. § 1901 et seq.) and California's own implementing statutes, Family Code § 177 and Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 224–224.6. Riley Lee's possible tribal affiliation, if known, is: Navajo Nation (or "not yet known"). My relationship to Riley Lee, if any, is: Parent. This information sheet explains, using the statutes' own text, California's Cal-ICWA inquiry, notice, active-efforts, and placement-preference requirements. It does not itself determine whether Riley Lee is in fact an Indian child, does not satisfy any court's, social worker's, or party's inquiry or notice obligation under these statutes, and does not substitute for a determination by the child's tribe, advice from a qualified attorney, or the court's own ruling. Only the court, following the statutory inquiry and notice process, can determine whether Cal-ICWA's heightened protections apply to Riley Lee's case.

WHICH PROCEEDINGS TRIGGER CAL-ICWA'S PROTECTIONS — FAMILY CODE § 177(A)-(C) AND THE “INDIAN CHILD CUSTODY PROCEEDING” DEFINITION IN FAMILY CODE § 170(C)
California Family Code § 177(a) provides: “In an Indian child custody proceeding, the court shall apply Sections 224.2 to 224.6, inclusive, and Sections 305.5, 361.31, and 361.7 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, and the following rules from the California Rules of Court, as they read on January 1, 2007: (1) Paragraph (7) of subdivision (b) of Rule 5.530. (2) Subdivision (i) of Rule 5.534.” Section 177(b) explains how these cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code provisions operate inside a Family Code case: “In the provisions cited in subdivision (a), references to social workers, probation officers, county welfare department, or probation department shall be construed as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption under this code.” Section 177(c) limits the whole rule to Indian-child cases: “This section shall only apply to proceedings involving an Indian child.” Family Code § 170(c) defines the triggering term itself: ““Indian child custody proceeding” means a “child custody proceeding” within the meaning of Section 1903 of the Indian Child Welfare Act, including a voluntary or involuntary proceeding that may result in an Indian child’s temporary or long-term foster care or guardianship placement if the parent or Indian custodian cannot have the child returned upon demand, termination of parental rights, or adoptive placement. An “Indian child custody proceeding” does not include a proceeding under this code commenced by the parent of an Indian child to determine the custodial rights of the child’s parents, unless the proceeding involves a petition to declare an Indian child free from the custody or control of a parent or involves a grant of custody to a person or persons other than a parent, over the objection of a parent.” Regarding Riley Lee, these Cal-ICWA protections accordingly apply only where the proceeding fits this statutory definition — not to every Family Code matter that happens to involve Riley Lee.

(2) Subdivision (i) of Rule 5.534."

An “Indian child custody proceeding” does not include a proceeding under this code commenced by the parent of an Indian child to determine the custodial rights of the child’s parents, unless the proceeding involves a petition to declare an Indian child free from the custody or control of a parent or involves a grant of custody to a person or persons other than a parent, over the objection of a parent."

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which proceedings trigger Cal-ICWA's heightened protections — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that every Family Code proceeding involving a family member who is an American Indian or Alaska Native triggers these protections. Three of these citations — Fam. Code § 177(a), § 177(b), and § 177(c) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 177); no additional independent source beyond § 177 itself was found for that group, so they are not independent of one another. The fourth citation, Fam. Code § 170(c), is a separate, independently numbered section and is independent of the § 177 group. Section 170(c)'s own definition cross-references 25 U.S.C. § 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act for the baseline “child custody proceeding” concept, and Family Code § 170(a) separately cross-references the same federal section for the definition of “Indian child” itself; this document does not independently verify or quote 25 U.S.C. § 1903's own text and relies only on the California statute's cross-reference to it. Family Code § 177(a) also directs application of Welfare and Institutions Code § 305.5, which this document does not address or verify. An ordinary custody dispute between two parents remains outside this definition unless it involves a petition to free the child from a parent's custody and control, or an award of custody to a nonparent over a parent's objection.

THE AFFIRMATIVE, CONTINUING DUTY TO INQUIRE WHETHER A CHILD IS OR MAY BE AN INDIAN CHILD — WELF. & INST. CODE § 224.2(A), (C)
Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(a) provides: “The court, county welfare department, and the probation department have an affirmative and continuing duty to inquire whether a child for whom a petition under Section 300, 601, or 602 may be or has been filed, is or may be an Indian child.” Section 224.2(c) extends that duty into the courtroom itself: “For a court presiding over any juvenile proceeding that could result in placement of an Indian child with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian, including proceedings where the parents or Indian custodian have voluntarily consented to placement of the child, the duty to inquire begins at the first hearing on a petition. At the commencement of the hearing, the court shall ask each party to the proceeding and all other interested persons present whether the child is, or may be, an Indian child, whether they know or have reason to know that the child is an Indian child, and where the child, the parents, or Indian custodian are domiciled, as defined in Section 224.1. Inquiry shall also be made at the first appearance in court of each party or interested person who was not present at the first hearing on the petition. The inquiry and responses shall occur on the record. The court shall instruct the parties and persons present to inform the court if they subsequently receive information that provides reason to know the child is, or may be, an Indian child.” By its own terms, § 224.2(a) attaches this duty to a juvenile-court petition filed under Welfare and Institutions Code § 300 (dependency), § 601, or § 602 (delinquency). When these same Welfare and Institutions Code sections are instead applied within a Family Code proceeding under Family Code § 177, § 177(b) — quoted in this document's companion scope clause — separately construes their references to social workers, probation officers, or county departments as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption; in that setting, the practical burden of inquiry falls on that party rather than on a county department.

“REASON TO KNOW” AN INDIAN CHILD IS INVOLVED — THE STATUTE'S OWN SIX TRIGGERING CIRCUMSTANCES, AND THE RESULTING NOTICE DUTY — WELF. & INST. CODE § 224.2(D), (F)
Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(d) does not leave “reason to know” to unconfirmed suspicion; it lists specific triggering circumstances: “There is reason to know a child involved in a proceeding is an Indian child under any of the following circumstances: (1) A person having an interest in the child, including the child, an officer of the court, a tribe, an Indian organization, a public or private agency, or a member of the child’s extended family informs the court that the child is an Indian child. (2) The residence or domicile of the child, the child’s parents, or Indian custodian is on a reservation or in an Alaska Native village, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1602 of Title 43 of the United State Code. (3) Any participant in the proceeding, officer of the court, Indian tribe, Indian organization, or agency informs the court that it has discovered information indicating that the child is an Indian child. (4) The child who is the subject of the proceeding gives the court reason to know that the child is an Indian child. (5) The court is informed that the child is or has been a ward of a tribal court. (6) The court is informed that either parent or the child possess an identification card indicating membership or citizenship in an Indian tribe.” Once any of these six circumstances exists, § 224.2(f) ties the inquiry to the notice duty: “If there is reason to know, as set forth in subdivision (d), that the child is an Indian child, the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian shall provide notice in accordance with Section 224.3.” Regarding Riley Lee, only one of these six specific, statutorily defined circumstances — not a general impression or unconfirmed guess — triggers the notice duty described in this document's companion clause on notice requirements.

(6) The court is informed that either parent or the child possess an identification card indicating membership or citizenship in an Indian tribe."

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific circumstances that trigger “reason to know” an Indian child is involved, and of the resulting notice duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that this list forecloses the court's, social worker's, or probation officer's separate duty of further inquiry on a lower “reason to believe” showing under § 224.2(e), which this clause does not quote and which does not by itself trigger the notice duty addressed here. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 224.2(d) and § 224.2(f); no additional independent source beyond § 224.2 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. Section 224.2(f)'s own text places the notice-sending duty specifically on “the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian,” not on the court itself; this clause does not resolve who that party is on any specific family's facts. This clause does not address § 224.2(g) through (k), covering the record the court must make when reason to know exists but membership is unconfirmed, the conclusive effect of a tribe's own determination, and a tribe's right to participate remotely, none of which was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document.

WHAT THE REQUIRED NOTICE MUST SAY AND HOW IT MUST BE SENT — WELF. & INST. CODE § 224.3(A)
Once notice is required, Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.3(a) states its own trigger, scope, and recipients: “If the court, a social worker, or probation officer knows or has reason to know, as described in subdivision (d) of Section 224.2, that an Indian child is involved, notice pursuant to Section 1912 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.) shall be provided for hearings that may culminate in an order for foster care placement, termination of parental rights, preadoptive placement, or adoptive placement, as described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 224.1. The notice shall be sent to the minor’s parents or legal guardian, Indian custodian, if any, and the child’s tribe. Copies of all notices sent shall be served on all parties to the dependency proceeding and their attorneys.” The same section also fixes the required delivery method: “Notice shall be sent by registered or certified mail with return receipt requested. Additional notice by first-class mail is recommended, but not required.”

This clause cites two provisions from the same statutory section, § 224.3(a)'s opening paragraph and § 224.3(a)(1); no additional independent source beyond § 224.3 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 224.3(a)(2) through (5), covering the tribal-chairperson service rule, the Secretary of the Interior notice requirement, and the detailed list of information the notice itself must contain (the child's name and birth information, known ancestor names, and a statement of the parents', Indian custodians', and tribe's rights to intervene, to petition for transfer to tribal court, and to appointed counsel, among other items), none of which was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document. This clause also does not address § 224.3(b) through the section's remaining subdivisions, covering timing before the hearing and related procedural requirements.

THE HEIGHTENED “ACTIVE EFFORTS” STANDARD FOR FOSTER CARE PLACEMENT AND TERMINATION OF PARENTAL RIGHTS — WELF. & INST. CODE § 361.7(A), (B)
Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.7(a) requires more than California's otherwise-applicable reasonable-efforts standard once an Indian child is involved: “Notwithstanding Section 361.5, a party seeking an involuntary foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights over, an Indian child shall provide evidence to the court that active efforts have been made to provide remedial services and rehabilitative programs designed to prevent the breakup of the Indian family and that these efforts have proved unsuccessful. The active efforts shall be documented in detail in the record.” Section 361.7(b) describes what “active efforts” requires, rather than leaving the term undefined: “What constitutes active efforts shall be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The active efforts shall be made in a manner that takes into account the prevailing social and cultural values, conditions, and way of life of the Indian child’s tribe. Active efforts shall utilize the available resources of the Indian child’s extended family, tribe, tribal and other Indian social service agencies, and individual Indian caregiver service providers.”

The active efforts shall be documented in detail in the record."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 361.7(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 361.7(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=361.7.)

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the heightened active-efforts standard and the statute's own description of what that standard requires — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that “active efforts” and the otherwise-applicable “reasonable efforts” standard under Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.5 are the same thing; § 361.7(a)'s own opening phrase, “Notwithstanding Section 361.5,” signals that active efforts is a distinct, higher standard, but this document does not independently verify or quote § 361.5's own text for comparison. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 361.7(a) and § 361.7(b); no additional independent source beyond § 361.7 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This clause does not address § 361.7(c), which separately requires a qualified-expert-witness determination, supported by clear and convincing evidence, before a foster care placement or guardianship may be ordered for an Indian child; the qualified-expert-witness definition itself appears in Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.6, which this document does not independently verify or quote.

THE STATUTORY PLACEMENT-PREFERENCE HIERARCHY FOR FOSTER CARE/GUARDIANSHIP AND ADOPTIVE PLACEMENTS — WELF. & INST. CODE § 361.31(B), (C)
For a foster care or guardianship placement of an Indian child, Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.31(b) sets a descending order of preference: “Preference shall be given to the child’s placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) A foster home licensed, approved, or specified by the child’s Indian tribe. (3) An Indian foster home licensed or approved by an authorized non-Indian licensing authority. (4) An institution for children approved by an Indian tribe or operated by an Indian organization that has a program suitable to meet the Indian child’s needs.” For an adoptive placement, § 361.31(c) sets a separate, shorter order: “In any adoptive placement of an Indian child, preference shall be given to a placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) Other members or citizens of the child’s Indian tribe. (3) Another Indian family.”

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the statutory placement-preference hierarchy for foster care/guardianship placements and for adoptive placements of an Indian child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 361.31(b) and § 361.31(c); no additional independent source beyond § 361.31 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This preference order is not absolute: § 361.31(d) lets a different order established by the child's own tribe take precedence, subject to full faith and credit; and § 361.31(h) through (j) let a party depart from the preference order on a showing of “good cause,” proven by clear and convincing evidence, based on specific considerations the statute lists (among them a parent's own informed request, the child's own request, a sibling attachment that can be maintained only through a particular placement, the child's extraordinary needs, or the unavailability of a suitable preferred placement after a diligent search). None of those subdivisions was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document, and this clause does not resolve whether good cause exists on any specific family's facts.

expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(a) provides: “The court, county welfare department, and the probation department have an affirmative and continuing duty to inquire whether a child for whom a petition under Section 300, 601, or 602 may be or has been filed, is or may be an Indian child.” Section 224.2(c) extends that duty into the courtroom itself: “For a court presiding over any juvenile proceeding that could result in placement of an Indian child with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian, including proceedings where the parents or Indian custodian have voluntarily consented to placement of the child, the duty to inquire begins at the first hearing on a petition. At the commencement of the hearing, the court shall ask each party to the proceeding and all other interested persons present whether the child is, or may be, an Indian child, whether they know or have reason to know that the child is an Indian child, and where the child, the parents, or Indian custodian are domiciled, as defined in Section 224.1. Inquiry shall also be made at the first appearance in court of each party or interested person who was not present at the first hearing on the petition. The inquiry and responses shall occur on the record. The court shall instruct the parties and persons present to inform the court if they subsequently receive information that provides reason to know the child is, or may be, an Indian child.” By its own terms, § 224.2(a) attaches this duty to a juvenile-court petition filed under Welfare and Institutions Code § 300 (dependency), § 601, or § 602 (delinquency). When these same Welfare and Institutions Code sections are instead applied within a Family Code proceeding under Family Code § 177, § 177(b) — quoted in this document's companion scope clause — separately construes their references to social workers, probation officers, or county departments as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption; in that setting, the practical burden of inquiry falls on that party rather than on a county department.

This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 224.2(a) and § 224.2(c); no additional independent source beyond § 224.2 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(d) does not leave “reason to know” to unconfirmed suspicion; it lists specific triggering circumstances: “There is reason to know a child involved in a proceeding is an Indian child under any of the following circumstances: (1) A person having an interest in the child, including the child, an officer of the court, a tribe, an Indian organization, a public or private agency, or a member of the child’s extended family informs the court that the child is an Indian child. (2) The residence or domicile of the child, the child’s parents, or Indian custodian is on a reservation or in an Alaska Native village, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1602 of Title 43 of the United State Code. (3) Any participant in the proceeding, officer of the court, Indian tribe, Indian organization, or agency informs the court that it has discovered information indicating that the child is an Indian child. (4) The child who is the subject of the proceeding gives the court reason to know that the child is an Indian child. (5) The court is informed that the child is or has been a ward of a tribal court. (6) The court is informed that either parent or the child possess an identification card indicating membership or citizenship in an Indian tribe.” Once any of these six circumstances exists, § 224.2(f) ties the inquiry to the notice duty: “If there is reason to know, as set forth in subdivision (d), that the child is an Indian child, the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian shall provide notice in accordance with Section 224.3.” Regarding Riley Lee, only one of these six specific, statutorily defined circumstances — not a general impression or unconfirmed guess — triggers the notice duty described in this document's companion clause on notice requirements.

expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.7(a) requires more than California's otherwise-applicable reasonable-efforts standard once an Indian child is involved: “Notwithstanding Section 361.5, a party seeking an involuntary foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights over, an Indian child shall provide evidence to the court that active efforts have been made to provide remedial services and rehabilitative programs designed to prevent the breakup of the Indian family and that these efforts have proved unsuccessful. The active efforts shall be documented in detail in the record.” Section 361.7(b) describes what “active efforts” requires, rather than leaving the term undefined: “What constitutes active efforts shall be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The active efforts shall be made in a manner that takes into account the prevailing social and cultural values, conditions, and way of life of the Indian child’s tribe. Active efforts shall utilize the available resources of the Indian child’s extended family, tribe, tribal and other Indian social service agencies, and individual Indian caregiver service providers.”

expectedJSON.body: For a foster care or guardianship placement of an Indian child, Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.31(b) sets a descending order of preference: “Preference shall be given to the child’s placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) A foster home licensed, approved, or specified by the child’s Indian tribe. (3) An Indian foster home licensed or approved by an authorized non-Indian licensing authority. (4) An institution for children approved by an Indian tribe or operated by an Indian organization that has a program suitable to meet the Indian child’s needs.” For an adoptive placement, § 361.31(c) sets a separate, shorter order: “In any adoptive placement of an Indian child, preference shall be given to a placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) Other members or citizens of the child’s Indian tribe. (3) Another Indian family.”

This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 361.31(b) and § 361.31(c); no additional independent source beyond § 361.31 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This preference order is not absolute: § 361.31(d) lets a different order established by the child's own tribe take precedence, subject to full faith and credit; and § 361.31(h) through (j) let a party depart from the preference order on a showing of “good cause,” proven by clear and convincing evidence, based on specific considerations the statute lists (among them a parent's own informed request, the child's own request, a sibling attachment that can be maintained only through a particular placement, the child's extraordinary needs, or the unavailability of a suitable preferred placement after a diligent search). None of those subdivisions was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document, and this clause does not resolve whether good cause exists on any specific family's facts.
